sources.entry: The KVM halt polling system - Defines the host-side polling after a vCPU halt that trades idle host CPU for guest wakeup time, unseen by the guest.

summary.title: The KVM halt polling system
summary.one_liner: KVM halt polling makes the host busy-poll for a short, adaptive interval after a guest vCPU halts, trading idle host CPU for lower wakeup latency.
takeaways: After a vCPU halts, the host polls for wakeup conditions for up to halt_poll_ns before calling the scheduler, saving a few microseconds of scheduler trip.

The polling interval adapts per vCPU: it grows (multiplied by halt_poll_ns_grow) when wakeups arrive just beyond it and shrinks (divided by halt_poll_ns_shrink) when block time exceeds the global max.

Module parameters halt_poll_ns, halt_poll_ns_grow, halt_poll_ns_grow_start and halt_poll_ns_shrink are system-wide, set via /sys/module/kvm/parameters/, unless a VM uses KVM_CAP_HALT_POLL for per-VM override.
Large halt_poll_ns values can drive host CPU usage to 100% on otherwise idle machines, so it is a power-versus-latency trade-off.
Polling stops immediately if another task becomes runnable on that CPU, so a guest cannot starve the host CPU.
summary.summary: This kernel documentation page describes KVM's halt polling feature, where the host polls for a guest wakeup for a limited time after a vCPU cedes the CPU, instead of immediately invoking the scheduler. It explains the generic implementation in kvm_vcpu_block() and the powerpc kvm-hv variant, and how the per-vCPU polling interval is grown and shrunk adaptively. A table lists the four tunable module parameters and their defaults, and the page ends with notes on CPU-usage trade-offs and the KVM_CAP_HALT_POLL per-VM override.
